anchors.fact: 1824: Elizabeth Heyrick of Leicester (1769–1831) wrote *Immediate, not Gradual Abolition* (F1, F2, F21, F22). She wrote that gradualism was "almost universal" among abolitionists, and that opposing it "may seem a most presumptuous, as well as hopeless attempt" (F11). Then she opposed it, telling her side they had shown "a great deal too much politeness" (F12)
anchors.meaning: the fuss made inside her own side, having named out loud how it would look
anchors.speaksTo: "causes a fuss to help care for people"; frightened and speaks anyway (her words are an argument, never a record of fear)

anchors.fact: Her ask of households: abstain from West Indian produce, "sugar, especially" (F4), and not by giving it up: "substitute East India for West India sugar" (F5); a sacrifice so small it seemed "almost burlesque" to call it one (F6)
anchors.meaning: outrage turned into one thing you can do on Monday
anchors.speaksTo: care made practical; no one left out of it

anchors.fact: She voices the doubt, what can "a few individuals, or a few families" do?, and answers "It can do wonders" (F7)
anchors.meaning: the powerlessness fear, answered in print
anchors.speaksTo: the fear that the fuss changed nothing

anchors.fact: She died in 1831; the Act of 1833 abolished slavery in the British colonies from 1 August 1834, "subject to" its obligations (F1, F10)
anchors.meaning: she never saw the end of hers
anchors.speaksTo: never gets to see the whole win → "count yours"

anchors.fact: The *Codex* Tom Collins (p. 138) with its simple syrup swapped for cane jaggery syrup: an Indian unrefined cane sugar (Oxford SUGAR pdf 1944; F15), less sweet than white sugar (pdf 1946; F16), 65–85% sucrose + 9–15% reducing sugars (F19). Close to "East India sugar", not the same (stand-in ruling)
anchors.speaksTo: "Nothing was given up. It just came from somewhere else."

anchors.fact: Blue glass sugar bowl, probably Bristol, c. 1820–30, gilt-lettered (V&A C.14-2023; F17), shown with **no legible letters**
anchors.meaning: the campaign carried to the tea table
anchors.speaksTo: care made visible in an ordinary room

cocktail.closingLine: Make it with the sugar you swapped. Then count the ones you've already won.
cocktail.glassware: a tall (Collins) glass, chilled, filled with ice
method: Make the syrup ahead. Grate or finely chop 100 g cane jaggery (sold in blocks as gur in Indian grocers), stir it into 100 ml warm water until it dissolves, and let it cool. Keep it in the fridge and use it within two weeks.
Chill a tall glass and pour the cold soda water into it.
Shake the gin, lemon juice and jaggery syrup with ice for about five seconds, just long enough to chill them.
Strain into the glass on top of the soda (the pour mixes it, so there's no need to stir), then fill the glass with ice.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Not Too Polite

recipe.note: the swap: an Indian cane sugar, made the old unrefined way, in place of white sugar. Some makers clean it with plant extracts, groundnut (peanut) among them, so it's marked nuts to be safe.

cocktail.tagline: You speak up for the people who aren't in the room.

reading.epigraph: Everything in this glass is ordinary except the sugar. The sugar is the argument.
whoYouAre: When something is unfair to someone who isn't in the room, yours is the voice that goes first. At the meeting, at the school gate, at the family table. People think it comes easily to you. It doesn't. Your heart is going before you open your mouth, you rehearsed it on the way there, and afterwards, when somebody says they wish they could do that, your hands are still shaking.

You'd do it again tomorrow. Keeping quiet would be the comfortable thing, and you can't be comfortable while someone is being forgotten. Somebody quieter in that room was relieved it was you. And when it's over, you don't stop to see what changed. You're already looking at the next thing that isn't fair, that's your purpose.
yours: In 1824, a woman in Leicester called Elizabeth Heyrick wrote a short pamphlet against slavery in Britain's colonies. Almost everyone in the movement, she wrote, wanted it to end slowly, step by step. She wrote that disagreeing with them might seem "a most presumptuous, as well as hopeless attempt". Then she spent the rest of the pamphlet disagreeing, and told her own side they'd shown "a great deal too much politeness".

What she asked of ordinary households was small. Not to give up sugar, only to change where it came from. She said the sacrifice was so slight it seemed "almost burlesque" to call it one. She asked what "a few individuals, or a few families" could possibly do, and answered: "It can do wonders." She died in 1831. Parliament passed the Act abolishing slavery in the British colonies two years later.

I like to think her heart was going when she wrote that first page, and that she wrote the rest of it all the same. You'd know the feeling. And I think you'd know the other part too: she never saw the end. Your wins mostly happen after you've moved on, in rooms you're no longer in.

So the cocktail I crafted for you is a classic, the kind anyone can make: gin, lemon, sugar and soda water in a tall glass over ice. I swapped the sugar as an ode to her courage. This one is jaggery, an Indian cane sugar made the old unrefined way. It's close to what she meant, not the same. But you can taste the difference: it's rounder and a little toasted. Nothing was given up. It just came from somewhere else.

Before the next thing that isn't fair, do what you never do, and count. The times you spoke first. The people who didn't have to be brave on their own. The things that are different now because you wouldn't be polite about them. She didn't live to see the end of hers. You're still here to count yours, and I wish you plenty.
